issues.legal_issue: Authentication of an executive order does not prevent judicial review of whether the order was made in accordance with law.
material_facts: The notification was expressed and authenticated as an order of the Governor in accordance with the applicable authentication rules.
The challenge alleged that the notification was invalid because the required governmental satisfaction and decision-making process had not occurred.
issues.conclusion: Authentication makes it conclusive that the order was made by the Governor, but it does not foreclose adjudication of whether the order was made in accordance with law.
issues.legal_principle: Article 166(2) of the Constitution protects an authenticated order from challenge on the ground that it was not made by the Governor; it does not make the order’s legal compliance conclusive. The Court followed R. Chitralekha v. State of Mysore, which discussed Dattatreya Moreshwar Pangarkar v. State of Bombay, State of Bombay v. Purshottam Jog Naik, and Ghaio Mall and Sons v. State of Delhi, and treated Article 166’s procedural requirements as directory rather than mandatory.

predicates.appeal_challenges_government_notificatio: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the validity of a government notification.
predicates.order_authenticated_as_governor_order: The government order was expressed and authenticated in the prescribed manner as an order made by the Governor.
predicates.challenge_alleges_illegal_process: The challenger alleges that the order was made through a process that did not comply with law.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an authenticated government notification on the ground of an illegal process, the order’s legality remains open to judicial review.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory decision assigned to the State Government need not reflect the Governor’s personal satisfaction when the matter is not one the Governor must decide in discretion.
material_facts: The statutory provision empowered the State Government to issue a notification if satisfied that land was needed or likely to be needed for a public purpose.
The relevant governmental business had been allocated to a minister and processed within the department by an authorized officer.
The matter was not one in which the Constitution required the Governor to act in discretion.
issues.conclusion: The Governor’s personal satisfaction was not required for the notification; the statutory satisfaction was that of the State Government.
issues.legal_principle: Articles 154 and 166(3) of the Constitution, read with the statutory assignment of the decision to the State Government and the applicable Rules of Business, allow governmental business to be carried on by ministers and authorized departmental officers. Personal satisfaction of the Governor is not required where the matter is not one the Governor must decide in discretion.

predicates.appeal_challenges_government_notificatio: The proceeding is an appeal challenging the validity of a government notification.
predicates.statute_assigns_satisfaction_to_state_go: The governing law assigns the relevant satisfaction and decision to the State Government.
predicates.matter_not_reserved_for_governor_discret: The matter is not one the Governor is constitutionally required to decide in discretion.
predicates.business_allocated_to_minister: The Governor’s business rules allocate the relevant governmental business to a minister.

issues.definition: When the law assigns satisfaction to the State Government, the matter is not reserved for the Governor’s discretion, and the business is allocated to a minister, the Governor’s personal satisfaction is not required.

issues.legal_issue: A preliminary land notification may be issued without ministerial consideration when the applicable standing order does not cover that stage and an authorized departmental officer handles the matter.
material_facts: The appeals challenged a notification issued under a land development law, rather than a proceeding under the general land acquisition law referred to in one standing-order item.
The lands had not been shown to be waste lands within the scope of another standing-order item.

Although the Land Planning Committee had recommended acquisition, the law did not require the State Government to consult the Committee before issuing the preliminary notification; the Committee’s statutory role began at a later stage.
The applicable standing order concerning cases proposed to be taken up by the Committee did not cover the preliminary notification stage.
The minister had authorized departmental handling of matters by subordinate officers, and an authorized officer issued the notification.
issues.conclusion: The preliminary notification was validly issued without being referred to the minister; the standing-order items relied on did not apply at that stage.
issues.legal_principle: Under Articles 166(3) of the Constitution and the Rules of Business, a minister may issue standing orders for the disposal of departmental business. Under sections 3, 4 and 5 of the West Bengal Land Development and Planning Act, 1948, the Land Planning Committee’s statutory role begins after the State Government’s preliminary notification, and the Act and Rules do not require consultation with the Committee before that notification. The Court held that the relevant standing-order item about Committee cases did not cover the preliminary notification; the land-acquisition item concerned acquisition under the Land Acquisition Act, and the waste-land item did not apply because the land had not been shown to be waste land.

predicates.appeal_challenges_preliminary_land_notif: The proceeding is an appeal challenging a preliminary notification in a land-development acquisition process.
predicates.general_land_acquisition_proceeding: The notification is part of a proceeding under the general law for land acquisition.
predicates.established_waste_land: The land has been established to be waste land covered by a standing-order category requiring ministerial attention.
predicates.committee_role_begins_after_notification: The statutory committee’s assigned role begins after the preliminary notification is issued.
predicates.no_required_committee_consultation_at_no: The governing law does not require the government to consult the statutory committee before issuing the preliminary notification.
predicates.authorized_officer_handles_notification: A departmental officer authorized under the applicable governmental arrangements handles and issues the notification.

issues.definition: When an appeal concerns a preliminary land notification outside the general land-acquisition category, the land is not established to be waste land, the committee’s role begins later without required prior consultation, and an authorized officer issues the notification, ministerial referral is not required and the notification is valid.
